newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudanese rebels say they advance on power plant.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese rebels say they advance on power plant.

text.p: Sudanese rebels have advanced to within 70 km (45 miles) of the Blue Nile capital Damazin, which supplies Khartoum with most of its electricity, a rebel spokesman in the Eritrean capital Asmara said on Monday.
The Sudanese government newspaper al-Sudan al-Hadith said the Sudanese army and paramilitary People's Defence Forces were advancing too, but it gave no details of their deployment.
It also said Ethiopian forces had abducted to Ethiopia 160 secondary school children from the border town of Kurmuk, which the Sudanese army lost on January 12.
Yassir Arman, spokesman for the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), told Reuters in Asmara that rebels from the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) were still advancing.
The rebels said on Sunday they had killed 150 government troops at the town of Keili, 100 km (60 miles) south of Damazin.

"We are moving towards Damazin. Actually we are now 70 km outside Damazin," Arman said. "We are doing our best. Our plan is being executed successfully so far. We are confident of getting to Damazin."
There was no independent confirmation of the rebel claim.

Damazin is about 480 km (300 miles) southeast of Khartoum and some 90 km (55 miles) west of the border with Ethiopia. Its dam and hydroelectric station on the Blue Nile supply the Sudanese capital with up to 80 percent of its power.
The fall of Kurmuk, a town of 15,000 people some 580 km (360 miles) southeast of Khartoum, marked the start of the rebel offensive, which was in its ninth day on Monday.

The Sudanese government newspaper said Ethiopian forces had stopped people leaving Kurmuk for government-held areas and had recruited some of them as helpers. They also captured the governor of Kurmuk province and some other local dignitaries.

The Sudanese government says Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are behind the attacks in the east. All other parties say they are the work of the Sudanese rebels, an alliance of northerners and southerners fighting to overthrow the Islamist government.
Arman said the joint Sudanese opposition had seized several towns and 11 garrisons in the Blue Nile area but the government only admits losing Kurmuk and Qeissan near the Ethiopian border.

The Egyptian government newspaper al-Ahram said on Monday that leaflets appeared in the streets of Khartoum on Sunday criticising the government's record since it seized power in 1989 and calling for mobilisation against it.

The leaflets were in the name of the old trade unions dissolved after the military coup and replaced by more pliant union leaders. The old unions, once a powerful force in Sudanese force, continue to operate under ground.
"The unions asked for forces to arise so that this regime will go to that they called the dustbin of history," it said.
In Cairo, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak discussed the situation in Sudan with senior ministers.
Information Minister Safwat Sherif said Mubarak again said Egypt would not interfere in Sudan's internal affairs because the conflict was between the rulers and opposition forces.

"Egypt rejects completely any attempt to divide Sudan," added the minister. Egypt's main concern in Sudan is for the waters of the Nile and it fears that an independent state in southern Sudan could complicate water supplies.
Mubarak turned down a request for help in the east by Sudanese Vice-President al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh last week.
A decisive factor in Egypt's position was remarks by Sudanese Islamist leader Hassan al-Turabi, published in a Kuwaiti newspaper and seen in Cairo as critical of Egypt.
Egypt blames Turabi, now the speaker of parliament, for helping the Egyptian Islamist militants who tried to assassinate Mubarak in Addis Ababa in 1995.
